explanations.explanation: The LORD tells Moses, Israel's leader, what Pharaoh, king of Egypt, will say: “They are wandering the land in confusion; the wilderness has boxed them in.” So Pharaoh will see a people with nowhere to go. It's like watching a driver circle the same block and assuming they have no clue. The LORD already knew what He was doing, and He told Moses ahead of time.

That's not what Pharaoh says. The LORD says Pharaoh will call them confused and boxed in by the wilderness. I think nobody looks at a crowd camped with a sea in front of them and thinks, "Now that's an army." Pharaoh's words are about people who look stuck.

Pharaoh says no such thing. The LORD tells Moses to have Israel turn back and camp by the sea, and Pharaoh's words are that they are wandering in confusion and the wilderness has boxed them in. Nobody in that verse says a word about going home to Egypt. They look stuck, and that's the whole comment.

God says the Egyptians “…will know that I am the LORD.” He says it again in verse 18, when He talks about being honored through Pharaoh, his chariots, and his horsemen. That's the same promise twice, so I'd say He wants it heard. Pharaoh had brought a whole army, and God still said it plainly.
Forget isn't the word. God says the Egyptians “…will know that I am the LORD.” He repeats it in verse 18, so He clearly means it. Forgetting would be the opposite of what He says is coming.

God doesn't say deny. He says the Egyptians “…will know that I am the LORD.” Knowing is something that happens to them, whether they like it or not. Not even Pharaoh's whole army gets to argue with that.

Pharaoh and his officials say, “We have released Israel from serving us.” The people who did the work are gone, and now they're counting what that costs them. It's the sound of a boss who just noticed the empty desks.
The text doesn't say that. What they say is “We have released Israel from serving us.” Their worry is about losing their workers. Egypt's gods never come up in that moment.
Nobody mentions tricks. Pharaoh and his officials say, “We have released Israel from serving us.” That's the regret out loud. Moses doesn't even show up in their sentence.

This one's close, but the text says more. Pharaoh “…took 600 of the best chariots, and all the other chariots of Egypt, with officers over all of them.” So the 600 best weren't the only ones. Pharaoh brought every chariot Egypt had. Nothing got left in the garage.

Right. Pharaoh “…took 600 of the best chariots, and all the other chariots of Egypt, with officers over all of them.” So the 600 were the best of the bunch, and the rest came along too. Every chariot of Egypt was in that line. That's a lot of chariots for one chase.

explanations.answer: Cry out to the LORD in terror
explanations.explanation: The Israelites “…were terrified and cried out to the LORD.” They looked up, saw the Egyptians marching after them, and their first move was to call out to Him. I'd say that's a good first move, even with the fear.

explanations.answer: Line up to fight the army
explanations.explanation: The text shows terror, not a battle line. They “…were terrified and cried out to the LORD.” No one grabs a weapon in that verse. They look up, see an army, and cry out.

Nobody scatters in this verse. The Israelites “…were terrified and cried out to the LORD.” Then they speak to Moses. The text gives us fear and a cry, and nothing about running off in every direction.

They really say it: “…it would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in the wilderness.” They also remind Moses of what they'd said back in Egypt: “Leave us alone…” I think fear can make even slavery sound like the easy option. Moses answers in the next verse: “Do not be afraid.”

They did say it. The people tell Moses, “…it would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in the wilderness.” That's how scared they were. Moses doesn't argue back, he just tells them not to be afraid.

Moses says, “for the Egyptians you see today, you will never see again.” That's a big promise to make with an army in sight. He says it right after telling them the LORD's salvation comes today. Stay tuned, because the sea will show what he means.

Moses really does say it: “for the Egyptians you see today, you will never see again.” He says it to people who are terrified of that exact army. And he says it right after telling them the LORD's salvation will come today.
Moses says, “The LORD will fight for you…” Israel isn't asked to win this one. The battle belongs to the LORD, and that's the comfort.
Moses says, “you need only to be still.” The people had been crying out and complaining, so being still was a big ask. Their job in that moment was to stand there and let the LORD work.

Close, but Moses says “be still,” not wait. The verse says they “…need only to be still.” I can see why wait comes to mind, since I stare at my oven timer like it owes me money. Still is the word Moses picks.
Busy isn't the word. Moses says they “…need only to be still.” Busy is more my style, with flour on my mustache and a timer going off every five minutes. Moses picks a different word for them.
Moses never mentions weapons here. He says the LORD will fight for them, and that they “…need only to be still.” That's the whole plan. No swords needed from the people.

explanations.answer: Stretch it out over the sea to divide it
explanations.explanation: The LORD says, “…lift up your staff and stretch out your hand over the sea and divide it…” Moses's part is to lift the staff and stretch out his hand. The LORD does the rest. A very simple instruction for a very big sea.

explanations.answer: Raise it toward the sky over Egypt
explanations.explanation: The LORD points Moses toward the sea, not the sky. He says to “…stretch out your hand over the sea and divide it…” Egypt is behind them in this scene. The work is in front of them, and it's wet.

explanations.answer: Lay it on the heads of the people
explanations.explanation: That's not in the verse. The LORD tells Moses to “…stretch out your hand over the sea and divide it…” His hand goes toward the water. The people just get told to go forward.

God says the Israelites can “…go through the sea on dry ground.” The text says it again in verses 22 and 29, so it's worth noticing. Dry ground, with walls of water on the right and on the left. I'd have rubbed my eyes twice.

Muddy sounds believable, but it's not what God says. He tells Moses the Israelites will go through the sea “…on dry ground.” (Exodus 14:16) Verses 22 and 29 say it again, with walls of water on both sides. Muddy would have meant a whole nation losing their sandals in the muck, and the text never has that problem. I think I'd have kept checking my feet the whole way across.
God doesn't say rocky. He says “…on dry ground.” and the text repeats it in verses 22 and 29. Dry is the word that sticks. That's a walk you could do in your good shoes.

True. The angel of God, who had gone before the camp, went behind them, and the pillar of cloud stood behind them too. The text says it “…came between the camps of Egypt and Israel.” So the cloud sat right between the two camps. And “…all night long neither camp went near the other.”

It's true. The angel of God, who had gone before the camp, “…withdrew and went behind them.” The pillar of cloud also moved from in front of them to behind them. So they moved to the back of the camp.

The cloud was between the two camps, and “…all night long neither camp went near the other.” So Egypt's army didn't close in that night. The army was close by, but it didn't come near. Whatever else happened, the cloud was standing in the way.
Right. The cloud “…came between the camps of Egypt and Israel.” and “…all night long neither camp went near the other.” The army wasn't closing in. The cloud stood between them, lighting the night.

“…all that night the LORD drove back the sea with a strong east wind that turned it into dry land.” The wind blew all night long. Then the waters were divided, and the Israelites went through on dry ground. My chef's hat would not have survived that night.

An earthquake is a big, dramatic guess, and I respect the drama. But the text says the LORD drove the sea back “…with a strong east wind…” (Exodus 14:21), and the wind blew all that night. The passage gives wind and nothing else. That's like blaming the mixer for a noise that was really the timer. Right sound, wrong machine.
The LORD did send hail on Egypt earlier (Exodus 9:23), but not here. At the sea, He drove the water back with “…a strong east wind…” Different moment, different tool.

The Israelites went through “…with walls of water on their right and on their left.” The text says it in verse 22 and again in verse 29. It's quite a hallway. Water on both sides, dry ground in the middle.

Fire is in this story, since the LORD looked down from the pillar of fire and cloud, but the walls are not fire. The text says “…walls of water on their right and on their left.” Water on both sides, and a path down the middle.
Not stone. The walls were “…walls of water on their right and on their left.” The song later says the Egyptians sank like a stone, but that's a different line. Here the walls are water.

The LORD “…caused their chariot wheels to wobble, so that they had difficulty driving.” Wobbly wheels are something anyone who has pushed a shopping cart can picture. Right after that, the Egyptians say, “…the LORD is fighting for them against Egypt!” The wheels were the problem, and the Egyptians noticed who was behind it.
The horses aren't what wobble. The LORD “…caused their chariot wheels to wobble, so that they had difficulty driving.” The trouble was in the wheels. The horses were still pulling.
Not the drivers. The text says He “…caused their chariot wheels to wobble…” and that's why they had difficulty driving. The wheels get the blame in the text. The drivers just get the difficulty.

The Egyptians say, “Let us flee from the Israelites, for the LORD is fighting for them against Egypt!” That's the Egyptians themselves saying it. It's the same thing Moses told Israel in 14:14. Even the army could see what was happening.
They do say it. The Egyptians cry, “Let us flee from the Israelites, for the LORD is fighting for them against Egypt!” These are the army's own words. They see who is fighting.

The waters covered the chariots and horsemen, “…the entire army of Pharaoh that had chased the Israelites into the sea. Not one of them survived.” This is a heavy part of the story. The text is plain about it, so I'll be plain too.

The text doesn't say that. It says the waters covered the chariots and horsemen, “…the entire army of Pharaoh that had chased the Israelites into the sea.” Then it says, “Not one of them survived.” No one is named as an exception. This part is heavy, and the text doesn't soften it.
No half in this verse. It says the waters covered the chariots and horsemen, “…the entire army of Pharaoh…” and “Not one of them survived.” That's a heavy part of the story. The text keeps it simple.

explanations.answer: They fear the LORD and believe in Him and Moses
explanations.explanation: The people “…feared the LORD and believed in Him and in His servant Moses.” They had just seen His great power over the Egyptians. After all that crying out and complaining, they believed. I love that.

explanations.answer: They build an altar right there on the shore
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention an altar. What it says is that the people “…feared the LORD and believed in Him and in His servant Moses.” Their response is in their hearts first. The singing comes next.

explanations.answer: They argue over who should lead them now
explanations.explanation: No arguing here. The people “…feared the LORD and believed in Him and in His servant Moses.” They trusted Moses as the LORD's servant. The only noise coming next is a song.

explanations.answer: Thrown horse and rider into the sea
explanations.explanation: The song says, “The horse and rider He has thrown into the sea.” That's the first thing it celebrates. Moses and the Israelites sing it right after crossing.

explanations.answer: Split the rock in the wilderness
explanations.explanation: That's not in this song. Moses and the Israelites sing to the LORD about what He did to Pharaoh's army: “The horse and rider He has thrown into the sea.” The rock and the wilderness don't come up in these lines. This song is about the sea.

explanations.answer: Sent frogs over the land of Egypt
explanations.explanation: Frogs belong to an earlier part of the Egypt story (Exodus 8:6). This song is about the sea. It says, “The horse and rider He has thrown into the sea.” Different chapter, different miracle.

The song says, “He is my God, and I will praise Him, my father’s God, and I will exalt Him.” So the song praises Him as the God of the singer's father too. It reaches back to the family before him. It's a short line with a lot of history.

It's in there. The song says, “He is my God, and I will praise Him, my father’s God, and I will exalt Him.” So the LORD is both the singer's God and his father's God. That line looks back at the family.

The song says, “Your right hand, O LORD, has shattered the enemy.” Notice the song stops talking about Him and starts talking straight to Him. The line right before it calls that hand “…majestic in power…” The word right hand shows up twice in one verse, so the song really wants us to look at His hand.

Moses did stretch out his hand over the sea (Exodus 14:21), but the song credits someone else. It says, “Your right hand, O LORD, has shattered the enemy.” The song points to the LORD's hand, not Moses's.

No swords from Israel in this part of the song. The only sword here is the enemy's, who says, “I will draw my sword…” (Exodus 15:9). The song says, “Your right hand, O LORD, has shattered the enemy.” The credit goes to the LORD.

explanations.answer: The blast of the LORD's nostrils
explanations.explanation: The song says, “At the blast of Your nostrils the waters piled up…” It's a picture of His power in the way a poem would put it. The currents stood firm “like a wall…”

explanations.answer: The stamp of the LORD's feet
explanations.explanation: The song doesn't say feet. It says, “At the blast of Your nostrils the waters piled up…” The piling up is credited to the LORD's blast. That's the picture the song paints.
The song doesn't credit Moses's voice. It says, “At the blast of Your nostrils the waters piled up…” The song gives the credit to the LORD. Moses is singing it.
The song says, “But You blew with Your breath, and the sea covered them.” The enemy had bragged about what they would do. The sea answers it. They “…sank like lead in the mighty waters.”
Not darkness. The song says, “…You blew with Your breath, and the sea covered them.” The cloud had even lit up the night earlier. In the song, it's the sea that covers them.
The cloud was there earlier, standing between the camps, but the song doesn't say that. It says, “…You blew with Your breath, and the sea covered them.” The sea is the one that does the covering.

The song asks, “Who among the gods is like You, O LORD?” and goes on, “Who is like You—majestic in holiness, revered with praises, performing wonders?” Asking it that way shows nobody is like Him. No god gets set beside Him. The question is its own answer.

Right. The song asks, “Who among the gods is like You, O LORD?” and then, “Who is like You—majestic in holiness, revered with praises, performing wonders?” The song asks it as a question with no one to name. So no god is on His level.

The LORD leads the people He has redeemed, and the song names the goal: “…Your holy dwelling.” I think that tells us the journey doesn't end at the sea. Verse 17 adds more, calling it the mountain of His inheritance and the sanctuary His hands have established. That's where the song is headed.

explanations.answer: To the banks of the Jordan
explanations.explanation: The song doesn't name the Jordan. It says He will guide them “…to Your holy dwelling.” Verse 17 adds more, speaking of the mountain of His inheritance and the sanctuary His hands have established. The song points to His place, not a river.

explanations.answer: To the shores of the Great Sea
explanations.explanation: The song doesn't say that. It says, “with Your strength You will guide them to Your holy dwelling.” The goal is His holy dwelling. Not another shoreline.

The song says the opposite. “The nations will hear and tremble; anguish will grip the dwellers of Philistia.” They'll be dismayed, not welcoming. The song doesn't have them coming out to greet anyone.

Right. The song says, “The nations will hear and tremble…” and that anguish will grip Philistia. Edom's chiefs will be dismayed and Moab's leaders will be seized with trembling. No welcome party in sight.
The song ends, “The LORD will reign forever and ever!” It's a big finish after a big song. It doesn't end with Egypt or the sea, it ends with Him.
Watch isn't the word. The song ends, “The LORD will reign forever and ever!” Reign is a king's word. The last line points to His rule.
Rest isn't the word. The song ends with “The LORD will reign forever and ever!” Reign is a king's word. The very last line is about His rule, and it has no end in it.

The text says Miriam the prophetess, Aaron's sister, “…took a tambourine in her hand, and all the women followed her with tambourines and dancing.” So the women are the ones who follow her. Then Miriam sings back to them. That's a lot of tambourines.
The elders aren't mentioned. The text says “…all the women followed her with tambourines and dancing.” Miriam leads and the women follow. It's a women's dance line.
Priests aren't mentioned here. The text says “…all the women followed her with tambourines and dancing.” Miriam plays and the women join her. That's who is dancing.
